growth_story.headline: Reforms and peace lifted Uganda's income per person 3.8 percent a year from 1990 to 2011; since 2012 it has grown 1.6 percent a year, and oil is close.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2011, Uganda's income per person grew 3.8 percent a year. The World Bank credits economic reforms, the end of the conflict with the Lord's Resistance Army and good outside conditions, including South Sudan as a new trading partner. From 2012 the pace fell to 1.6 percent a year, as reform momentum slowed, outside conditions turned and droughts hit, while public investment became the main engine of the growth that remained. A fast-growing population meant that growth in the whole economy turned into only modest gains per person, with small falls in 2017 and 2020. Income per person then grew 3.2 percent in 2024 and 3.5 percent in 2025, when it reached its highest level yet. The World Bank now expects oil revenue to start in 2027, while public debt and the cost of servicing it have risen.

threads.title: Reforms and peace drive the boom
threads.text: In the 1990s and 2000s Uganda steadied its economy, freed prices and the exchange rate, and sold or closed loss-making state firms. The end of the conflict with the Lord's Resistance Army and new regional markets, including South Sudan, added to growth.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe Uganda's recent growth as strong, yet income per person grew only 1.6 percent a year from 2012 to 2025 and 1.7 percent a year from 2016 to 2025. Much of the gap is population growth: the World Bank notes that growth in the whole economy after 2011 only just outpaced it, so the strong headline figures overstate the gains for the average person.
